translations.answer: The user claims to use wider friction randomization, ensures dynamic friction does not exceed static friction, configures actuators with an actuator-net, and sets the physics dt to be approximately 10 times faster than the policy dt; the reward table simultaneously increases air_time/foot_clearance and includes action_smoothness and foot_slip. The deployment uses ONNX Runtime and Docker custom scripts. Threads are only as described by the author, without independent replication, and specific weights cannot be directly transplanted into Go2 or humanoid robots.
translations.applicability: Unitree Go1 personal engineering record; only as a starting point for Go2/footed system experiments.
translations.credibility.rationale: Environmental, processing steps, and results have engineering records, but formal cross-validation or independent replication is missing.
translations.details.attempts.0: The user randomized foot static friction between 0.8–2.0 and dynamic friction between 0.6–1.6.
translations.details.attempts.1: The contributor notes the difference between Isaac Gym's average and Isaac Lab locomotion examples when combined.
translations.details.attempts.2: Go1 users report using a wider friction range, actuator-net, a physics/policy frequency ratio of approximately 10x, and specific foot reward settings.
translations.details.diagnostics.1: Check foot contact sensor and air-time reward.
translations.details.diagnostics.2: Compare friction randomization range, reward terms, actuator model, and policy/physics dt.
translations.details.environments.0: Isaac Lab locomotion; Unitree Go2 question environment; community Go1/ANYmal-D experience; specific Isaac Lab commit not mentioned.
translations.details.limits.0: Mixing Go2, Go1, and ANYmal-D threads; numerical values cannot be directly transplanted between robots.
translations.details.limits.1: Community users explicitly state some suggestions are based on personal testing or not yet tested; the post lacks a unified closed-loop.
translations.details.outcomes.0: The user claims friction randomization helps and achieves initial Go2 Sim-to-Real, but still tends to fall.
translations.details.outcomes.1: Go1 users report good transferability and reduced foot slip, but no independent replication.
translations.details.problem_statements.0: The simulation strategy relies on dragging feet, but fails to move when deployed on Go2.
translations.details.problem_statements.1: Foot friction randomization allows initial transfer, but gait remains unnatural and prone to falling.
translations.details.suspected_causes.0: The friction combine mode in simulation differs from the assets/rewards used, making dragging feet a exploitable behavior.
translations.details.suspected_causes.1: The actuator model does not match real-world dynamics.
translations.details.symptoms.0: Simulation feet do not lift, dragging the ground.
translations.details.symptoms.1: Real-world strategy fails to move or easily falls.
translations.details.symptoms.2: Friction randomization leads to pronking-like gait.
